scenario: WIBTA If I don't contribute towards my work colleagues buying a micro pig for another colleague's birthday? | Tldr: my colleagues bought me fish which I wasn't expecting in the past for my birthday. Another colleague's birthday is coming up and they want to buy them a pig and I don't really agree. WIBTA if I don't contribute? I really wish this was a joke but let me explain. This colleague of mine is about to turn 40. We will call them George if that's okay. Nothing against her she is a great person. Now George still lives at home with their parents and owns a dog. They are going through the phase of desperately dating around, and they have always wanted a micro pig. My colleagues love to celebrate birthdays. They bought me fish, bless them, for my 20th birthday because I was very lonely at the time as I had just moved out from my parents house etc. I really appreciated the thought and I love my fish dearly, but sometimes I feel a little bit tied down by them, as I'm not always at home (I spend a lot of time around my boyfriend 's house) and one day I eventually want to move away and that may be an issue with fish as if be looking to go to another house share. Don't get me wrong I really really appreciated the thought, but I don't think they took into consideration the commitment it takes to look after an animal. They did mean we'll though. Although I expressed slight interest in what I would hypothetically name an axolotl before my birthday, I never ever expected to see fish when I walked into my room. I am currently in a house share with a colleague, as it was the only viable option at the time. Back to George, my concern is they still live at home and it really isn't fair on their parents to bring a surprise pig into the house. I'm also concerned about how the pig will interact with the dog. If course I want to celebrate their birthday, but I just simply don't agree with buying someone a micro pig without taking into consideration the commitments that go into looking after them. Besides little guppies are very different to a micro pig. So will I be the asshole if I just buy my own gift for them?

First, I need to understand the core tension here. The user feels conflicted because:
- Colleague's group wants to buy a micro pig for George (40, lives with parents, has a dog)
- User previously received fish as a surprise gift which they appreciated but now find problematic (commitment issues, potential future moving)
- User genuinely doesn't think a micro pig is appropriate for George's situation (parents' home, dog compatibility, high commitment)
- They want to celebrate George but refuse to participate in this specific gift

Hmm... the "WIBTA" (Would I Be The Asshole) framing is interesting. The user isn't asking " is this ethical?" but specifically " will people see me as the jerk for opt out?" That's key. 

Looking deeper at their reasoning:
- They're not against celebrating George ( "I want to celebrate their birthday")
- Their objection is purely about the * appropriateneness* of a micro pig as a gift
- They've thought about animal welfare (parents' home, dog interaction, commitment level)
- They're aware their fish gift was well-intentioned but still problematic - showing they're not just being nitpicky

*Pausing to fact-check micro pig realities*... 
- "Micro pig" is a myth (they grow to 150+ lbs)
- Most places require permits for exotic pets
- Pig-dog cohabitation is high-risk (predatory instinct)
- 40yo living with parents likely has no space for a pig
- This gift is objectively ill-advised. 

*User's position*:
- "I don't agree with buying a micro pig without considering commitments" - this is actually responsible. 
- They're not being "the asshole" by refusing; they're being the voice of reason. 
- The fish example shows they understand * well-intentioned but impractical gifts can backfire* - so their concern is valid.

*Social dynamics angle*:
- In group gifting, people often feel pressured to contribute even when uncomfortable
- But "I don't want to be part of this" is a valid boundary, especially when the gift could harm someone
- Colleague's "we bought you fish" argument doesn't hold water - that was their choice, not a obligation to reciprocate with similarly problematic gifts

*Final judgment*:
- Not only is it * not* asshole behavior to opt out - it's * responsible* to opt out
- The real "asshole" would be someone who contributes knowing it's a bad idea
- User should absolutely buy a different gift (e.g., "I'm getting George X instead - would you like to join?")

*Why 1 (not asshole)*:
- They're acting in George's best interest (preventing a potentially harmful gift)
- They're not being mean - just declining participation in something they believe is wrong
- The fish example actually *supports* their position (they're aware of how "surprise pets" can backfire)

*Additional nuance*:
- If the group proceeds without them, that's on the group - not the user
- Their "I'll buy my own gift" plan is actually the * most considerate* approach (celebrate without enabling a bad idea)

*Final answer*: 1 (not asshole)
